text: Overview
html: Overview

text: MIRACLE is a government-funded interdisciplinary research project focused on developing robotic systems to assist individuals with walking impairments. As a member of the Robotics Team at Yonsei University's MLCS Lab, I contributed to the mechanical development of a pediatric lower-limb exoskeleton, from CAD design to fabrication and assembly.
html: MIRACLE is a government-funded interdisciplinary research project focused on developing robotic systems to assist individuals with walking impairments. As a member of the Robotics Team at Yonsei University's MLCS Lab, I contributed to the mechanical development of a pediatric lower-limb exoskeleton, from CAD design to fabrication and assembly.

text: Building on the physical prototype, I modeled the exoskeleton's dynamics and investigated sensorless impedance control. I subsequently designed a disturbance-observer-enhanced control architecture and evaluated its tracking performance in MATLAB simulations.
html: Building on the physical prototype, I modeled the exoskeleton's dynamics and investigated sensorless impedance control. I subsequently designed a disturbance-observer-enhanced control architecture and evaluated its tracking performance in MATLAB simulations.

text: Two-Link Dynamic Model
html: Two-Link Dynamic Model

text: I then constructed a double-pendulum model and derived its dynamics using the Euler–Lagrange formulation. Based on the Jacobian matrices of each link's center of mass and their rotational inertias, I obtained the following inertia matrix.
html: I then constructed a double-pendulum model and derived its dynamics using the Euler–Lagrange formulation. Based on the Jacobian matrices of each link's center of mass and their rotational inertias, I obtained the following inertia matrix.

text: Using the inertia matrix, I derived the Coriolis and centrifugal matrix through the Christoffel symbols of the first kind. This matrix describes the velocity-dependent forces and dynamic coupling between the hip and knee joints.
html: Using the inertia matrix, I derived the Coriolis and centrifugal matrix through the Christoffel symbols of the first kind. This matrix describes the velocity-dependent forces and dynamic coupling between the hip and knee joints.

text: I then derived the gravitational vector from the potential energy of both links. By differentiating the potential energy with respect to the joint angles, I obtained the gravitational torque acting on each joint.
html: I then derived the gravitational vector from the potential energy of both links. By differentiating the potential energy with respect to the joint angles, I obtained the gravitational torque acting on each joint.

text: Finally, I combined the inertia, Coriolis and centrifugal, and gravitational terms to obtain the complete equation of motion for the two-link exoskeleton.
html: Finally, I combined the inertia, Coriolis and centrifugal, and gravitational terms to obtain the complete equation of motion for the two-link exoskeleton.

text: This model describes the joint dynamics under applied and external disturbance torques and provided the foundation for developing the sensorless impedance controller and disturbance observer.
html: This model describes the joint dynamics under applied and external disturbance torques and provided the foundation for developing the sensorless impedance controller and disturbance observer.

text: ROB-Based Sensorless Impedance Control
html: ROB-Based Sensorless Impedance Control

text: For a wearable robot, following a predefined trajectory alone is insufficient. The robot must also respond to external forces generated through interaction with the wearer.
html: For a wearable robot, following a predefined trajectory alone is insufficient. The robot must also respond to external forces generated through interaction with the wearer.

text: To address this, I implemented a sensorless impedance control framework based on a Reaction Torque Observer (ROB), following the approach proposed by Tran et al. Instead of relying on additional force/torque sensors, the ROB estimates external interaction torque using motor encoder feedback and the robot's dynamic model.
html: To address this, I implemented a sensorless impedance control framework based on a Reaction Torque Observer (ROB), following the approach proposed by Tran et al. Instead of relying on additional force/torque sensors, the ROB estimates external interaction torque using motor encoder feedback and the robot's dynamic model.

text: ROB-Based Sensorless Impedance Control Architecture
html: ROB-Based Sensorless Impedance Control Architecture

text: (Adapted from Tran et al. https://doi.org/10.1109/AIM.2015.7222611)
html: (Adapted from Tran et al. https://doi.org/10.1109/AIM.2015.7222611)

text: Based on the derived dynamic model, I formulated the external torque estimation process under the model compensation assumptions. However, directly differentiating encoder measurements can amplify noise. To address this, the ROB uses a low-pass filter to estimate external interaction torque while reducing the effects of measurement noise.
html: Based on the derived dynamic model, I formulated the external torque estimation process under the model compensation assumptions. However, directly differentiating encoder measurements can amplify noise. To address this, the ROB uses a low-pass filter to estimate external interaction torque while reducing the effects of measurement noise.

text: I then incorporated the estimated interaction torque into the desired impedance model. By defining the desired inertia, damping, and stiffness, the controller can adjust the exoskeleton's mechanical response to external interaction.
html: I then incorporated the estimated interaction torque into the desired impedance model. By defining the desired inertia, damping, and stiffness, the controller can adjust the exoskeleton's mechanical response to external interaction.

text: Using the impedance tracking error, I derived the commanded acceleration and joint torque to achieve trajectory tracking while maintaining the desired impedance behavior.
html: Using the impedance tracking error, I derived the commanded acceleration and joint torque to achieve trajectory tracking while maintaining the desired impedance behavior.

text: Although this framework enables sensorless impedance control, its performance can be affected by uncertainties in the dynamic model. During the development of the baseline controller, I observed a delay between the reference gait trajectory and the actual joint motion. This motivated me to investigate an additional disturbance compensation method to improve tracking performance.
html: Although this framework enables sensorless impedance control, its performance can be affected by uncertainties in the dynamic model. During the development of the baseline controller, I observed a delay between the reference gait trajectory and the actual joint motion. This motivated me to investigate an additional disturbance compensation method to improve tracking performance.

text: Disturbance Observer-Enhanced Robust Control
html: Disturbance Observer-Enhanced Robust Control

text: To address this, I integrated a nonlinear Disturbance Observer (DO) into the existing ROB-based sensorless impedance control framework.
html: To address this, I integrated a nonlinear Disturbance Observer (DO) into the existing ROB-based sensorless impedance control framework.

text: Unlike previous approaches that combine the two observers in parallel, I proposed a serial architecture in which the DO first estimates and compensates for disturbances and model uncertainties. The ROB then estimates the remaining external interaction torque using the compensated system dynamics.
html: Unlike previous approaches that combine the two observers in parallel, I proposed a serial architecture in which the DO first estimates and compensates for disturbances and model uncertainties. The ROB then estimates the remaining external interaction torque using the compensated system dynamics.

text: My goal was to improve the accuracy of external torque estimation and reduce trajectory-tracking errors.
html: My goal was to improve the accuracy of external torque estimation and reduce trajectory-tracking errors.

text: Proposed serial DO–ROB control architecture. The DO compensates for disturbances and model uncertainties before the ROB estimates the remaining external interaction torque.
html: Proposed serial DO–ROB control architecture. The DO compensates for disturbances and model uncertainties before the ROB estimates the remaining external interaction torque.

text: Starting from the previously derived equation of motion, I formulated the disturbance model and designed a nonlinear observer to estimate the disturbance torque.
html: Starting from the previously derived equation of motion, I formulated the disturbance model and designed a nonlinear observer to estimate the disturbance torque.

text: To avoid directly using joint acceleration measurements, which can amplify encoder noise through numerical differentiation, I introduced an auxiliary vector. This allowed me to formulate the observer using the robot's dynamic model and joint velocity information.
html: To avoid directly using joint acceleration measurements, which can amplify encoder noise through numerical differentiation, I introduced an auxiliary vector. This allowed me to formulate the observer using the robot's dynamic model and joint velocity information.

text: I then designed the auxiliary function based on the joint velocities and derived the corresponding observer gain matrix using the inertia matrix.
html: I then designed the auxiliary function based on the joint velocities and derived the corresponding observer gain matrix using the inertia matrix.

text: By substituting the auxiliary function into the observer formulation, I derived the observer dynamics without explicitly requiring joint acceleration measurements.
html: By substituting the auxiliary function into the observer formulation, I derived the observer dynamics without explicitly requiring joint acceleration measurements.

text: The estimated disturbance can then be reconstructed from the auxiliary vector and the designed function. This estimate is used for disturbance compensation in the proposed controller.
html: The estimated disturbance can then be reconstructed from the auxiliary vector and the designed function. This estimate is used for disturbance compensation in the proposed controller.

text: To ensure that the disturbance observer could provide a reliable estimate, I further analyzed its estimation-error dynamics using Lyapunov theory. This analysis allowed me to derive a sufficient condition for selecting the observer gain based on the mechanical parameters of the exoskeleton.
html: To ensure that the disturbance observer could provide a reliable estimate, I further analyzed its estimation-error dynamics using Lyapunov theory. This analysis allowed me to derive a sufficient condition for selecting the observer gain based on the mechanical parameters of the exoskeleton.

text: Lyapunov-Based Stability Analysis
html: Lyapunov-Based Stability Analysis

text: To examine the stability of the proposed disturbance observer, I first defined the disturbance estimation error as the difference between the actual and estimated disturbances.
html: To examine the stability of the proposed disturbance observer, I first defined the disturbance estimation error as the difference between the actual and estimated disturbances.

text: Assuming that the disturbance remains approximately constant over the observer's estimation timescale, I derived the estimation-error dynamics. This provided the foundation for analyzing whether the observer error converges to zero.
html: Assuming that the disturbance remains approximately constant over the observer's estimation timescale, I derived the estimation-error dynamics. This provided the foundation for analyzing whether the observer error converges to zero.

text: To analyze the estimation-error dynamics, I introduced a coordinate transformation of the inertia matrix. This allowed me to express the observer dynamics in a form suitable for Lyapunov analysis.
html: To analyze the estimation-error dynamics, I introduced a coordinate transformation of the inertia matrix. This allowed me to express the observer dynamics in a form suitable for Lyapunov analysis.

text: Using the transformed inertia matrix, I constructed a positive-definite Lyapunov candidate function to examine the convergence of the disturbance estimation error.
html: Using the transformed inertia matrix, I constructed a positive-definite Lyapunov candidate function to examine the convergence of the disturbance estimation error.

text: I then differentiated the Lyapunov function with respect to time and substituted the estimation-error dynamics.
html: I then differentiated the Lyapunov function with respect to time and substituted the estimation-error dynamics.

text: By expressing its derivative as a quadratic form, I examined the conditions required for the derivative to remain negative definite. This led to a sufficient observer gain condition based on the mechanical parameters and the maximum angular velocity of the second link.
html: By expressing its derivative as a quadratic form, I examined the conditions required for the derivative to remain negative definite. This led to a sufficient observer gain condition based on the mechanical parameters and the maximum angular velocity of the second link.

text: The resulting condition relates the observer gain to the mass, geometry, and maximum angular velocity of the second link.
html: The resulting condition relates the observer gain to the mass, geometry, and maximum angular velocity of the second link.

text: Under the assumptions used in the analysis, satisfying this condition provides a sufficient basis for asymptotic convergence of the disturbance estimation error.
html: Under the assumptions used in the analysis, satisfying this condition provides a sufficient basis for asymptotic convergence of the disturbance estimation error.

text: This analysis allowed me to establish a theoretical criterion for selecting the observer gain rather than relying solely on empirical tuning. The proposed controller was subsequently evaluated through MATLAB simulations.
html: This analysis allowed me to establish a theoretical criterion for selecting the observer gain rather than relying solely on empirical tuning. The proposed controller was subsequently evaluated through MATLAB simulations.

text: The animated plot below compares the reference trajectory and the simulated joint response for the hip and knee joints. Compared with the ROB-only baseline, the DO+ROB controller followed the reference trajectory more closely, particularly at the knee joint.

text: Impedance Behavior under External Disturbances
html: Impedance Behavior under External Disturbances

text: To evaluate whether the proposed DO+ROB controller could maintain the desired impedance behavior under external disturbances, I conducted additional MATLAB simulations using two impedance settings: Soft and Stiff.
html: To evaluate whether the proposed DO+ROB controller could maintain the desired impedance behavior under external disturbances, I conducted additional MATLAB simulations using two impedance settings: Soft and Stiff.

text: I applied simulated random disturbances and compared the joint responses under different damping and stiffness parameters while maintaining the same desired inertia. The Soft setting was designed to allow greater compliance, whereas the Stiff setting was intended to provide greater resistance to external disturbances.
html: I applied simulated random disturbances and compared the joint responses under different damping and stiffness parameters while maintaining the same desired inertia. The Soft setting was designed to allow greater compliance, whereas the Stiff setting was intended to provide greater resistance to external disturbances.

text: Simulation parameters
html: Simulation parameters

text: The results showed that the Soft setting allowed larger deviations from the reference trajectories, while the Stiff setting maintained closer tracking, particularly at the hip joint. This behavior was consistent with the expected relationship between mechanical impedance and disturbance response.

This behavior was consistent with the expected relationship between mechanical impedance and disturbance response.

text: The RMS tracking errors further confirmed these differences. Overall, the simulations demonstrated that the proposed DO+ROB controller retained the expected impedance-dependent behavior under external disturbances.

text: ☑️Robust Control & Stability Analysis
html: ☑️Robust Control & Stability Analysis

text: To address the observed trajectory-tracking delay, I proposed a serial DO–ROB control architecture and derived the corresponding disturbance observer equations. I analyzed the observer's estimation-error convergence using Lyapunov theory and evaluated the proposed controller through MATLAB simulations, achieving 14.7% and 27.4% reductions in RMS tracking error at the hip and knee joints, respectively.
html: To address the observed trajectory-tracking delay, I proposed a serial DO–ROB control architecture and derived the corresponding disturbance observer equations. I analyzed the observer's estimation-error convergence using Lyapunov theory and evaluated the proposed controller through MATLAB simulations, achieving 14.7% and 27.4% reductions in RMS tracking error at the hip and knee joints, respectively.
